text: The latest development in the ransomware world is CryptoWall 2.0, a new version of this malware family that uses the Tor network for command and control.

text: F-Secure was the first to spot this new version on October 1, but since then the attacks have ramped up and new variants of the malware are emerging daily.

text: Our WildFire analysis platform has picked up 84 CryptoWall 2.0 variants since September 30, delivered primarily through e-mail attachments but also through malicious PDFs and web exploit kits.

text: CryptoWall 2.0 is similar to other ransomware attacks that have plagued users and businesses for nearly a decade.

text: Once it is running on a system, CryptoWall 2.0 seeks out document files and encrypts them using the RSA encryption algorithm.
label: malware

text: The attacker holds the key necessary to decrypt the files unless the victim agrees to pay a $500 ransom.  Unlike previous versions of CryptoWall, 2.0 communicates with its command and control (C2) server through the Tor anonymization network.
label: malware

text: CryptoWall isn’t the only threat that communicates over Tor and if your network doesn’t have an explicit reason to allow anonymization networks, you should consider blocking the application altogether with your firewall.

text: Yesterday, TrustedSec, a security consultancy based on Ohio, wrote that the recent breach at Community Health Systems (CHS) was the result of exploitation of the Heartbleed OpenSSL vulnerability (CVE-2014-0160).
label: TIME

text: CHS’s 8-K filing on Monday did not reveal how the attackers got into their network, only that the records of approximately 4.5 million patients were stolen in attacks in between April and June of 2014.
label: identity

text: TrustedSec reports on how attackers were apparently able to glean user credentials from a certain device via the Heartbleed vulnerability and use them to log in via a VPN.
label: identity

text: We need more facts to be sure, but this instance may be the first public breach related to the Heartbleed vulnerability since it was announced in April.
label: TIME

text: Now, over four months since the Heartbleed disclosure, this attack reminds us of how serious this vulnerability is and how critical protection against it remains.
label: vulnerability

text: As Heartbleed allows the attacker to scrape memory from the vulnerable device, they can retrieve significant amounts of secret information.
label: attack-pattern

text: In this case, that apparently included VPN credentials, which they then used to log into the network and more laterally from system to system until discovering the data they were after.
label: SOFTWARE

text: As the OpenSSL library is so widely used, some administrators may be finding unpatched systems for years to come.
label: SOFTWARE

text: While network-based defenses are not a substitute for patching software, Heartbleed is detectable using IPS signatures.
label: vulnerability

text: Palo Alto Networks deployed five signatures in April to defend against this threat, 40039, 36420, 36419, 36418 and 36416.
label: identity

text: No matter how well patched your systems are, there’s no reason not to deploy IPS signatures like these to detect and block attempted Heartbleed exploits.
label: vulnerability

text: A Heartbleed probe could be evidence of the early stages of an attack on your network, and persistent attackers are unlikely to give up after jiggling the handle on the front door.

text: As shoppers and retailers gear up for the 2017 holiday season, they need to be aware of a new kind of cybersecurity threat they may face this year: unauthorized coin mining.
label: attack-pattern

text: Unauthorized coin mining is a new threat that can affect retailers and shoppers in a way that could impact or even halt their online shopping experience.
label: attack-pattern

text: A recent Unit 42 threat intelligence posting on the topic showed how 63 percent of the unauthorized coin mining sites we found came online in October 2017.
label: identity

text: This surge in unauthorized coin mining is driven, in large part, by the recent skyrocketing in the value of digital currencies like bitcoin.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Unlike other cybersecurity threats we’re used to bracing for around the holiday season, unauthorized coin mining attacks can affect shoppers who are up-to-date with security patches and even some running some security protections.
label: attack-pattern

text: And unlike spam or phishing, these attacks also don’t require any lapse in vigilance by the user: they can happen simply by going to websites users know and trust.
label: attack-pattern

text: And for shoppers, the impact of a successful attack is minimal: there are no lasting effects or impact, making it an annoyance at worst.  But because of the potential impact on holiday shopping and the ease of attacks, unauthorized coin mining is an attack that retailers need to be aware of and take active steps for prevention this holiday season.
label: attack-pattern

text: What Is Unauthorized Coin Mining?
label: attack-pattern

text: The best way to understand the threat of unauthorized coin mining is to first understand its impact.
label: attack-pattern

text: Unauthorized coin mining is an attack that can cause a user’s system to suddenly and unexpectedly slow down, sometimes significantly, when visiting a website.
label: attack-pattern

text: What causes this impact is when the website the user visits is running “coin miner” code.
label: malware

text: “Coin miner” code is code used to “mine” for digital currency like bitcoin.
label: malware

text: How Do Unauthorized Coin Mining Attacks Happen?
label: attack-pattern

text: Unauthorized coin mining attacks happen very simply: the website the user is visiting has special code on it that performs coin mining operations on the visitor’s computer while they’re on the website.
label: attack-pattern

text: When unauthorized coin mining happens with the site owner’s knowledge and permission, it’s basically a malicious site.
label: attack-pattern

text: And for the shopper, it means you’re on an untrustworthy site and so open to all manner of risks beyond just unauthorized coin mining.
label: attack-pattern

text: The real, significant situation shoppers and retailers need to think about this season is when unauthorized coin mining code is on a site without that site owner’s knowledge and permission.
label: attack-pattern

text: In our latest Unit 42 research on cybercriminals using the Hancitor malware, we show that not only are their attacks about business, we can see these cybercriminals deftly applying some fundamental business principles around timing, specialization, and globalization.
label: identity

text: Hancitor is a malware that focuses getting other malware onto the victim’s system.
label: malware

text: In the case of Hancitor, it’s typically banking Trojans that steal the victim’s banking information.
label: malware

text: In our latest research, we can see the attackers behind Hancitor have been timing their attacks to happen during the busiest time of the global working week, the middle of the week.
label: malware

text: Hancitor isn’t particularly advanced in its tactics: it’s ideal target is an old or outdated version of Microsoft Windows like Windows 7 or even Windows XP.
label: malware

text: As you can see in Figure 1 below, throughout 2017, the Hancitor attacks show clear spikes in their occurrence and these spikes happen during the middle of the week.
label: TIME

text: Figure 1: Timeline of Hancitor campaign activity since January 2017.
label: malware

text: The attackers behind Hancitor aren’t the first to time their spam attacks like this, but it is an effective tactic to try and increase their chances of success, especially when combined with the other innovation that we’ve seen.
label: malware

text: In the past, Hancitor was sent as a malicious attachment in a spam email which would then download and install the attackers’ final malware like a banking Trojan.
label: malware

text: When they would do this, the Hancitor attachment would download and install the final malware from a malicious or compromised site.
label: malware

text: But as organizations have gotten more effective at blocking malicious attachments like Hancitor, we’ve seen the attackers behind Hancitor adapt to evade detection and prevention.
label: malware

text: They’ve done this by moving the Hancitor malware from being a malicious attachment in spam to itself being a malicious download.
label: malware

text: The spam the attackers use no long has a malicious attachment but instead a malicious link that downloads the malicious Hancitor attachment.
label: malware

text: Figure 2 shows one of these that was made to look like an Amazon shipping notice.
label: identity

text: Figure 2: Hancitor malspam example from February 2017.
label: malware

text: This means that a Hancitor attack now has two downloads rather than one and what these attackers did around the malicious downloads shows another modern business tactic: globalization.
label: malware

text: Globalizing the Attacks  Figure 3 below is a map showing where our Unit 42 researchers have found webistes involved in Hancitor attacks.
label: malware

text: Figure 3: Hancitor distribution servers globally thus far in 2017  Table 1 – Number of Distribution Servers by Country
label: malware

text: The hot spots in the United States represents distribution servers which are created using fraud based accounts at various hosting providers that are hosting the Hancitor documents while the hotspots in Asia represent legitimate sites for small and medium businesses that have been compromised by the actors behind Hancitor campaign to host the malicious Hancitor documents.
label: malware

text: What is most interesting about Hancitor is the way these decisions so clearly reflect an awareness of business realities (by targeting peak working times) and dividing up the “work” of their attacks in a way that so clearly mirrors mainstream business decisions around globalizing operations.
label: malware

text: In the end, while Hancitor may not be sophisticated, these steps to adapt and stay effective seem to be succeeding.
label: malware

text: And we expect to continue to see Hancitor be a global threat for the foreseeable future.
label: malware

text: In the months since the WanaCrypt0r/WannaCry and the Petya/NotPetya attacks, security researchers have delved into the nuts and bolts these incidents and the malware involved.
label: malware

text: One key thing that research into these security incidents shows is that these attacks used a relatively new and unknown technique called kernel APC attacks as part of their toolkit.
label: attack-pattern

text: Kernel APC attacks occur in a way that increases the “stealth” factor and makes standard detection and prevention very difficult.
label: attack-pattern

text: And kernel APC attacks do this while still maximizing the power and control that the code has on the target system.
label: attack-pattern

text: While kernel APC attacks aren’t well known and can be hard to understand, their proven success in WanaCrypt0r/WannaCry and the Petya/NotPetya make them an important threat to understand because proven attack techniques are quickly adopted widely.
label: malware

text: To understand what makes kernel APC attacks so dangerous, it’s important to understand what they are.  The kernel is the heart of the operating system.
label: attack-pattern

text: When talking about operating systems with security permissions and controls like Windows or UNIX/Linux, the kernel operates with the highest level of control.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Because of this, attacks against the kernel are used to gain complete control over a system, generally as part of an “elevation or privilege” (EoP) or “privilege escalation” attack.
label: attack-pattern

text: Privilege escalation attacks against the kernel have been around for some time and are well-known and can be well protected against.  Kernel APC attacks however are a different class of attack.
label: attack-pattern

text: Instead kernel APC attacks already have kernel privileges and use them to further carry out their attack.
label: attack-pattern

text: In this case by making legitimate programs execute malicious code rather than their own legitimate code.
label: attack-pattern

text: Kernel APC attacks do this using their control over the kernel to redirect APCs: “Asynchronous Procedure Calls”.
label: attack-pattern

text: In a kernel APC attack, the attacker gives a legitimate program’s place in line to the attacker’s code.
label: attack-pattern

text: Taken altogether, these make kernel APC attacks an effective and sophisticated technique.
label: attack-pattern

text: And while this technique alone isn’t solely responsible for the damaging power of WanaCrypt0r/WannaCry and Petya/NotPetya it is certainly an important contributing factor.

text: Following a recent study of apps in the Google Play Store, let’s discuss several security risks caused by the bad certificate management practiced in many Android apps, from social to mobile banking.

label: identity

label: SOFTWARE

text: They are the equivalent of LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress in Windows.

And that credential theft is a key element in each stage:  It’s also worth noting that credentials are a keystone issue in Shamoon 2 wave 2 too: we saw evidence of targeting an organization’s virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) solutions with default credentials.

text: This post is also available in:      日本語 (Japanese)  The Lapsus$ Group threat actor has grown in just a few months from launching a handful of destructive attacks to stealing and publishing source code of multiple top-tier technology companies.
label: threat-actor

text: Though sometimes called a ransomware group in reports, Lapsus$ is notable for not deploying ransomware in extortion attempts.
label: threat-actor

text: Lapsus$, however, is unusual in its approach – for this group, notoriety most often appears to be the goal, rather than financial gain.
label: threat-actor

text: Unit 42 has helped organizations respond to multiple Lapsus$ attacks.
label: identity

text: The Lapsus$ Group doesn’t employ malware in breached victim environments, doesn’t encrypt data and in most cases, doesn’t actually employ extortion.
label: attack-pattern

text: They focus on using a combination of stolen credentials and social engineering to gain access to victims.
label: attack-pattern

text: We’ve also seen them solicit employees on Telegram for their login credentials at specific companies in industries including: telecom, software, gaming, hosting providers and call centers.
label: SOFTWARE

text: In addition, we’ve seen destructive Lapsus$ attacks where the actors got access to an organization’s cloud environment, wiped systems and destroyed over a thousand virtual machines.
label: threat-actor

text: Although there are no public indicators of compromise (IoCs), and no tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) that are unique to Lapsus$ Group, here we will summarize what is known of this threat actor to better enable defenders in understanding and mitigating this threat.
label: threat-actor

text: Early Targets of Lapsus$ Evolution of Targeted Organizations Mitigation Actions Conclusion
label: threat-actor

text: We first observed the “Lapsus$” handle mid-2021, but the first attack activity quoting that handle was in August 2021, with some U.K. mobile phone customers reporting receiving threatening texts (Figure 1).
label: threat-actor

text: In December 2021, the Ministry of Health of Brazil fell victim to an attack claimed by Lapsus$ (Figure 2).
label: TIME

text: This was followed in short order by attacks on South American telecoms providers Claro and Embratel, Brazilian state-owned postal service “Correios,” and Portuguese media giant Impresa.
label: location

text: This initial focus has led to speculation that Lapsus$ Group may be Brazilian, although we understand the choice of targets to have been influenced by extended team members rather than the team leadership.
label: threat-actor

text: Apart from Argentinian eCommerce provider Mercado Libre / Mercado Pago, subsequent victimology has departed South America and pivoted to focus on the high-tech sector.  Recent public victims have included:  It should be understood that in addition there are likely any number of other victims, targeted by attacks not known in the public sphere.
label: location

text: For example, in the “proof” of the Okta breach posted on the Lapsus$ Group’s Telegram channel, the actor states: “… our focus was ONLY on okta customers” (Figure 3)
label: identity

text: Several of the Lapsus$ Group’s attacks involved the theft and publication of source code.
label: threat-actor

text: In the case of Nvidia, it was observed as a non-financial extortion attempt.
label: identity

text: In other cases, for example that of Microsoft, there was simply publication without extortion, again supporting the understanding that the primary motivation of this actor is notoriety rather than financial gain.
label: identity

text: Owing to the diversity of techniques used, and the lack of use of malware, there is no single defense against or detection of Lapsus$ attacks specifically.
label: threat-actor

text: If Lapsus$ has purchased credentials for a network, they can effectively operate as an insider threat, taking advantage of the same privileges the employee has inside the network.  Focus on general information security best practices: MFA, access controls and network segmentation.
label: threat-actor

text: Patching of internal systems that might support lateral movement and privilege escalation should be prioritized, as well as against known public exploits that these actors might employ.
label: attack-pattern

text: Although the commodity malware RedLine Stealer has been implicated for credential harvesting in some attacks, it’s unclear if this is first- or third-party, and it cannot be used as a definitive indicator of Lapsus$-specific activity.

text: This post is also available in:      日本語 (Japanese)  Around 6:00 am PST on September 24, the details of a vulnerability in the widely used Bourne Again Shell (Bash) were disclosed by multiple Linux vendors.
label: TIME

text: The vulnerability, assigned CVE-2014-6271 by Mitre, was originally discovered by Stephane Chazelas, a Unix and Linux network and telecom administrator and IT manager at UK robotics company SeeByte, Ltd.
label: identity

text: While this vulnerability didn’t come with quite the fanfare or a catchy name like Heartbleed, the security community quickly dubbed it “Shellshock.”
label: vulnerability

text: Bash is present in most Linux and Unix distributions as well as Apple’s Mac OS X, and there’s a good chance anyone reading this has a system they need to patch.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Palo Alto Networks initiated an emergency IPS content release to detect this vulnerability last night with Signature ID: 36729 "Bash Remote Code Execution Vulnerability.”
label: identity

text: All versions of PAN-OS and Panorama include the vulnerable version of Bash, but we’ve determined the issue is only exploitable by authenticated users.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Normal PAN-OS maintenance release updates will provide a fix for the vulnerability.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Vulnerability Details  CVE-2014-6271 exists in all versions of Bash and is related to how environment variables are processed when the shell starts up.
label: vulnerability

text: In addition to storing variables, Bash allows for storing shell functions in variables that users can call later.
label: SOFTWARE

text: It’s in parsing these functions that the new Bash vulnerability exists, as the shell mistakenly executes code that is added after a function definition.
label: tools

text: At first glance, this might not seem too dangerous as executing commands is Bash’s primary function, but it’s important to understand that many other programs use Bash to process commands.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Bash is the default shell for the most-popular Linux variants and every version of the software stretching back over two decades is vulnerable.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Fortunately, not every system is remotely exploitable simply because it’s running Bash, it also needs to be running an application which makes Bash accessible over the network.
label: tools

text: As described above, the most-common exploit scenario seems like it will be web servers running Apache and using CGI scripts.
label: SOFTWARE

text: We discovered a new malware that targets online gambling companies in China via a watering hole attack, in which visitors are tricked into downloading a malware loader disguised as a legitimate installer for well-known apps such as Adobe Flash Player or Microsoft Silverlight.
label: attack-pattern

text: Closer examination of the loader shows that it loads either a Cobalt Strike shellcode or a previously undocumented backdoor written in Python, a new type of malware that we found to be named BIOPASS RAT (remote access trojan).
label: tools

text: BIOPASS RAT possesses basic features found in other malware, such as file system assessment, remote desktop access, file exfiltration, and shell command execution.
label: malware

text: What makes BIOPASS RAT particularly interesting is that it can sniff its victim’s screen by abusing the framework of Open Broadcaster Software (OBS) Studio, a popular live streaming and video recording app, to establish live streaming to a cloud service via Real-Time Messaging Protocol (RTMP).
label: malware

text: In addition, the attack misuses the object storage service (OSS) of Alibaba Cloud (Aliyun) to host the BIOPASS RAT Python scripts as well as to store the exfiltrated data from victims.
label: malware

text: We consider BIOPASS RAT as still being actively developed.
label: malware

text: Many of the loaders that we found were used to load Cobalt Strike shellcode by default instead of the BIOPASS RAT malware.
label: tools

text: Furthermore, BIOPASS RAT also creates scheduled tasks to load the Cobalt Strike shellcode during the initialization, indicating that the malicious actor behind the attack still heavily relies on Cobalt Strike.
label: malware

text: We also found several clues that show how the malware might be connected with the Winnti Group(also known as APT41).
label: threat-actor

text: In this blog entry, we will dive deeper into BIOPASS RAT with a detailed technical analysis of the infection chain, the different components of the malware, and any possible associations with Winnti.
label: threat-actor

text: Blackgear (also known as Topgear and Comnie) is a cyberespionage campaign dating back to 2008, at least based on the Protux backdoor used by its operators.
label: campaign

text: In 2016, for instance, we found their campaigns attacking Japanese organizations with various malware tools, notably the Elirks backdoor.
label: TIME

label: threat-actor

text: A notable characteristic of Blackgear is the degree to which its attacks are taken to evade detection, abusing blogging, microblogging, and social media services to hide its command-and-control (C&C) configuration.
label: attack-pattern

text: Compared to when C&C information is embedded within the malware, where it’s preset and can thus be easily blocked, this tactic lets Blackgear’s operators to quickly change C&C servers as needed.
label: threat-actor

text: It can, in turn, prolong the campaign’s foothold in the system and enable attackers to carry out further lateral movement.
label: attack-pattern

text: Spear Phishing is a specific attack technique that has become widely used in the past few years.
label: attack-pattern

text: In our new research blog “FreeMilk: A Highly Targeted Spear Phishing Campaign”, our Unit 42 research team has discovered an attack campaign that takes spear phishing targeting to the next level by hijacking in-progress email conversations.
label: identity

text: While these are not broad attacks, they represent an escalation in attacker spear phishing techniques in a way that makes it even more important than ever to have a prevention framework in place.
label: attack-pattern

text: Standard phishing attacks are broad attacks that use general email messages to carry out the attacks.
label: attack-pattern

text: Standard phishing attacks aren’t personalized: they use very common themes or lures in a generalized way in conjunction with a large enough pool of targets.
label: attack-pattern

text: The idea is that by chance some percentage of the phishing emails will look legitimate enough to the recipient to be successful.
label: attack-pattern

text: Basically, standard phishing attacks rely on the law of averages for its success.
label: attack-pattern

text: A good example of a generalized phishing campaign is the Blank Slate Campaign we wrote about in March 2017.
label: campaign

text: Spear phishing is a more refined and focused version of phishing.
label: attack-pattern

text: Instead of using generalized themes or lures, spear phishing uses themes or lures that are in some way relevant or appropriate for the target recipient.
label: attack-pattern

text: For example, a spear phishing attack could use email messages about military exercises sent to military or government targets like we saw with our recent research into CMSTAR Trojan attacks.
label: attack-pattern

text: Spear phishing focuses on the quality of the theme and lure where standard phishing focuses on quantity.
label: attack-pattern

text: Spear phishing is a suitable tactic when an attacker cares about who falls for it.
label: attack-pattern

text: Where a phishing attack campaign may send malicious emails out to thousands or tens of thousands of targets, a spear phishing campaign my send out just one malicious email to one target.
label: attack-pattern

text: Sometimes, when that target is a high-value target this attack can also be referred to as ‘Whaling”.  In our new research, our Unit 42 research team has found an attack that takes the refining of spear phishing one step further.
label: identity

text: If Charlie was successful in crafting the attack email to seem legitimate enough, Bob will open the email and any attachments and the attack will succeed.  Unlike phishing or even general spear phishing, this is a highly sophisticated, labor intensive, focused attack.
label: attack-pattern

text: Carrying out a successful conversation hijacking spear phishing attack requires knowing someone that the ultimate target is communicating with, compromising that person’s account, identifying an ongoing email conversation with the ultimate target, crafting an email to appear part of that ongoing email conversation and finally sending it.
label: attack-pattern

text: The specific attack our Unit 42 research team has seen using this technique relied on an attack against a vulnerability in Microsoft Office for which a patch is available.
label: identity

text: Second, using security on your systems, devices and networks that provides multiple layers of protection can help prevent attacks.  Conversation hijacking spear phishing isn’t a threat everyone faces, but for those who do it represents a significant escalation in terms of sophistication and social engineering of spear phishing attacks.
label: attack-pattern

text: It also takes spear phishing attacks to a level that makes it nearly impossible to distinguish an attack email from a legitimate email.
label: attack-pattern

text: Among these cybercriminals are financially motivated threat groups Carbanak and FIN7.
label: threat-actor

text: Although both names have at times been used to refer to the same group, organizations such as MITRE identifies them as two separate entities that wield the Carbanak backdoor in their attacks.
label: identity

text: However, the groups use not just the Carbanak backdoor but also other types of malware such as Pillowmint, a point-of-sale malware, and Tirion, which is said to be geared to replace Carbanak.
label: malware

text: MITRE also identifies different main targets for each group: While Carbanak focuses on banking institutions, FIN7 targets food, hospitality, and retail establishments.
label: threat-actor

text: This week, the results of this year's round of the MITRE Engenuity ATT&CK Evaluations were released, which focused on Carbanak+FIN7.
label: identity

text: We also separately discussed how Trend Micro solutions deal with these threats.
label: identity

text: For more background on what happens in attacks launched by Carbanak and FIN7, we pieced together information from our studies of these groups as well as information from ATT&CK tactics and techniques (a total of 65 techniques across 11 tactics) identified by MITRE to be related to these threat groups.
label: threat-actor

text: What happens in Carbanak and FIN7 attacks?
label: threat-actor

text: In our analysis of a related past campaign, we observed that attackers enter the system through spear phishing.
label: attack-pattern

text: After gaining a foothold in the system, the dynamic data exchange (DDE) feature in Windows and legitimate cloud-based services will then be abused to deliver the malware or to establish command-and-control (C&C) communication.
label: SOFTWARE

text: After this, the Carbanak backdoor can then be used to log keystrokes and capture screenshots, steal and delete cookies, inject malicious code on sites, and monitor various traffic.
label: malware

text: For lateral movement, the malware abuses remote and system administration tools.
label: attack-pattern

text: To be more specific in terms of ATT&CK® techniques, Carbanak and FIN7 share a notable number of similarities.
label: threat-actor

text: Figure 1. ATT&CK® tactics shared between Carbanak and FIN7      The following are the tactics and techniques that are employed by Carbanak and FIN7, as shared by MITRE.
label: threat-actor

text: Both groups use spear-phishing campaigns with attachments that are embedded with exploits as an entry point to the target system.
label: attack-pattern

text: For code and behavior execution, both groups use a variety of techniques through native API, PowerShell, service execution, user execution, Windows Component Object Model (COM) and Distributed COM, and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
label: tools

text: Carbanak also abuses command-line interface and DDE client-server protocol.
label: threat-actor

text: On the other hand, FIN7 takes advantage of Mshta, a utility that can execute VBScript, and scheduled tasks to run malicious code on user systems.
label: threat-actor

text: We detected a variant of the Carbanak malware that adds registry entries and keys as an autostart technique.
label: malware

text: In the case of FIN7, the use of application shimming databases (which can allow developers to apply fixes to applications without rewriting code) and hooking processes that allow the modification of program behaviors are some of the techniques that can be applied.
label: threat-actor

text: The former has been utilized in a campaign involving the Pillowmint malware.
label: malware

text: Privilege Escalation
label: attack-pattern

text: To elevate privileges, the groups bypass Windows User Account Control (UAC) mechanisms, new services, and valid accounts to elevate process privileges.
label: attack-pattern

text: For the same purpose, on Linux systems, Carbanak attacks can use sudo, a program that permits users to execute the programs of a superuser.
label: threat-actor

label: attack-pattern

label: threat-actor

text: Based on our investigation, we found that the intrusion process used by Earth Centaur can be separated into several stages, which are shown in Figure 1.
label: threat-actor

text: We found that the threat actors used vulnerable Internet Information Services (IIS) server and Exchange server vulnerabilities as entry points, and then installed web shells.
label: vulnerability

text: Afterward, the .NET loader (detected as Nerapack) and the first stage backdoor (Quasar remote administration tool aka Quasar RAT) were deployed on the compromised machine.

text: The following testimony was delivered to the U.S. House Intelligence Committee by Shane Huntley, Senior Director of Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) on July 27, 2022.  Chairman Schiff, Ranking Member Turner, and esteemed Members of the Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to appear before the Committee to discuss Google’s efforts to protect users from commercial spyware.
label: identity

text: Google has been tracking the activities of commercial spyware vendors for years, and we have been taking critical steps to protect our users.
label: identity

text: Our Threat Analysis Group, or TAG, is dedicated to protecting users from threats posed by state-sponsored malware attacks and other advanced persistent threats.
label: identity

text: TAG actively monitors threat actors and the evolution of their tactics and techniques.
label: identity

text: For example, TAG has been closely tracking and disrupting campaigns targeting individuals and organizations in Ukraine, and frequently publishes reports on Russian threat actors.
label: identity

text: TAG tracks and proactively counters serious state-sponsored and financially motivated information cyber criminal activities, such as hacking and the use of spyware.
label: identity

text: We are joined in this effort by many other security teams at Google, including Project Zero, our team of security researchers at Google who study zero-day vulnerabilities in the hardware and software systems that are depended upon by users around the world.
label: identity

text: Google has a long track record combating commercial surveillance tools targeting our users.
label: identity

text: In 2017, Android – which is owned by Google – was the first mobile platform to warn users about NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware.
label: malware

text: At the time, our Android team released research about a newly discovered family of spyware related to Pegasus that was used in a targeted attack on a small number of Android devices.
label: malware

text: We remediated the compromises for these users and implemented controls to protect all Android users.
label: SOFTWARE

text: NSO Group continues to pose risks across the Internet ecosystem.
label: threat-actor

text: In 2019, we confronted the risks posed by NSO Group again, relying upon NSO Groups’s marketing information suggesting that they had a 0-day exploit for Android.
label: threat-actor

text: Google was able to identify the vulnerability in use and fix the exploit quickly.
label: identity

text: In December 2021, we released research about novel techniques used by NSO Group to compromise iMessage users.
label: TIME

text: iPhone users could be compromised by receiving a malicious iMessage text, without ever needing to click a malicious link.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Short of not using a device, there is no way to prevent exploitation by a zero-click exploit; it's a weapon against which there is no defense.
label: attack-pattern

text: Based on our research and findings, we assessed this to be one of the most technically sophisticated exploits we had ever seen, further demonstrating that the capabilities NSO provides rival those previously thought to be accessible to only a handful of nation states.
label: threat-actor

text: Although this Committee must be concerned with the exploits of NSO Group, it is not the only entity posing risks to our users.
label: threat-actor

text: For example, TAG discovered campaigns targeting Armenian users which utilized zero-day vulnerabilities in Chrome and Internet Explorer.
label: campaign

text: Reporting by CitizenLab linked this activity to Candiru, an Israeli spyware vendor.
label: identity

text: Other reporting from Microsoft has linked this spyware to the compromise of dozens of victims, including political dissidents, human rights activists, journalists, and academics.
label: identity

text: Most recently, we reported in May on five zero-day vulnerabilities affecting Chrome and Android which were used to compromise Android users.
label: SOFTWARE

text: We assess with high confidence that commercial surveillance company Cytrox packaged these vulnerabilities, and sold the hacking software to at least eight governments.
label: threat-actor

text: Our reporting is consistent with earlier analysis produced by CitizenLab and Meta.
label: identity

text: TAG also recently released information on a segment of attackers we call “hack-for-hire” that focuses on compromising accounts and exfiltrating data as a service.
label: attack-pattern

text: In contrast to commercial surveillance vendors, who we generally observe selling a capability for the end user to operate, hack-for-hire firms conduct attacks themselves.
label: attack-pattern

text: In June, we provided examples of the hack-for-hire ecosystem from India, Russia, and the United Arab Emirates.
label: location

text: The growth of commercial spyware vendors and hack-for-hire groups has necessitated growth in TAG to counter these threats.
label: attack-pattern

text: Where once we only needed substreams to focus on threat actors such as China, Russia, and North Korea, TAG now has a dedicated analysis subteam dedicated to commercial vendors and operators.
label: location

text: Seven of the nine zero-day vulnerabilities our Threat Analysis Group discovered in 2021 were originally developed by commercial providers and sold to and used by state-sponsored actors.
label: identity

text: TAG is actively tracking more than 30 vendors with varying levels of sophistication and public exposure selling exploits or surveillance capabilities to state-sponsored actors.
label: identity

text: Last year, TAG identified an ongoing campaign targeting security researchers working on vulnerability research and development at different companies and organizations.
label: identity

text: The actors behind this campaign, which we attributed to a government-backed entity based in North Korea, have employed a number of means to target researchers.
label: campaign

text: While vulnerability research is an important contributor to online safety when that research is used to improve the security of products, vendors stockpiling zero-day vulnerabilities in secret can pose a severe risk to the Internet when the vendor itself gets compromised.
label: attack-pattern

text: This is why when Google discovers these activities, we not only take steps to protect users, but also disclose that information publicly to raise awareness and help the entire ecosystem, in line with our historical commitment to openness and democratic values.
label: identity

text: Across all Google products, we incorporate industry-leading security features and protections to keep our users safe.
label: identity

text: On Search, Google’s Safe Browsing is an industry-leading service to identify unsafe websites across the web and notify users and website owners of potential harm.
label: identity

text: Google Safe Browsing helps protect over four billion devices every day by showing warnings to users when they attempt to navigate to unsafe sites or download harmful files.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Safe Browsing also notifies webmasters when their websites are compromised by malicious actors and helps them diagnose and resolve the problem so that their visitors stay safer.
label: SOFTWARE

text: On Gmail, we recommend certain Gmail security precautions to prevent spoofing, phishing, and spam.
label: identity

text: By default, Gmail displays warnings and moves untrustworthy emails to the user’s spam folder.
label: SOFTWARE

text: For Android, through its entire development lifecycle, we subject the products to a rigorous security program.
label: SOFTWARE

text: The Android security process begins early in the development lifecycle, and each major feature of the platform is reviewed by engineering and security resources.
label: SOFTWARE

text: During the development stage, Android-created and open source components are subject to vigorous security reviews
label: SOFTWARE

text: For users, Android provides safety and control over how apps and third parties can access the data from their devices.
label: SOFTWARE

text: We have also built additional tools to prevent successful attacks on devices that run Android once those devices are in users’ hands.
label: SOFTWARE

text: For example, Google Play Protect, our built-in malware protection for Android, continuously scans devices for potentially harmful applications.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Google manages a vulnerability rewards program (VRP), rewarding researchers millions of dollars for their contributions in securing our devices and platforms.
label: identity

text: This is all part of a larger strategy to keep Google products and users, as well as the Internet at large more secure.
label: identity

text: Google developed Project Shield, a free protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, to protect news media and human rights organization websites.
label: attack-pattern

text: We recently expanded eligibility to protect Ukraine government organizations, and we are currently protecting over 200 Ukraine websites today.
label: identity

text: APP has a strong track record protecting users – since the program’s inception, there are no documented cases of an account compromise via phishing.
label: attack-pattern

text: We appreciate the Committee’s focus on this issue, and recommend the U.S. Intelligence Community prioritize identifying and analyzing threats from foreign commercial spyware providers as being on par with other major advanced threat actors.
label: identity

text: The U.S. could also set an example to other governments by reviewing and disclosing its own historical use of these tools.
label: identity

text: We welcome recent steps taken by the government in applying sanctions to the NSO Group and Candiru, and we believe other governments should consider expanding these restrictions.
label: threat-actor

text: Additionally, the U.S. government should consider a full ban on Federal procurement of commercial spyware technologies and contemplate imposing further sanctions to limit spyware vendors’ ability to operate in the U.S. and receive U.S. investment.
label: identity

text: Google is investing heavily as a company and as an industry to counter serious threats to our users.
label: identity

text: Google is committed to leading the industry in detecting and disrupting these threats.
label: identity

text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) continues to closely monitor the cybersecurity environment in Eastern Europe with regard to the war in Ukraine.
label: identity

text: Many Russian government cyber assets have remained focused on Ukraine and related issues since the invasion began, while Russian APT activity outside of Ukraine largely remains the same.
label: location

text: TAG continues to disrupt campaigns from multiple sets of Russian government-backed attackers, some of which are detailed in our previous updates.
label: identity

text: Similarly, Russian observed disinformation efforts are also focused on the war in Ukraine and TAG has disrupted coordinated influence operations from several actors including the Internet Research Agency and a Russian consulting firm as detailed in the TAG Bulletin.
label: threat-actor

text: Here is a deeper look at some campaign activity TAG has observed since our last update: Turla, a group publicly attributed to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), recently hosted Android apps on a domain spoofing the Ukrainian Azov Regiment.
label: identity

text: This is the first known instance of Turla distributing Android-related malware.
label: threat-actor

text: The apps were not distributed through the Google Play Store, but hosted on a domain controlled by the actor and disseminated via links on third party messaging services.
label: SOFTWARE

text: We believe there was no major impact on Android users and that the number of installs was miniscule.
label: SOFTWARE

text: The app is distributed under the guise of performing Denial of Service (DoS) attacks against a set of Russian websites.
label: attack-pattern

text: However, the 'DoS' consists only of a single GET request to the target website, not enough to be effective.
label: attack-pattern

text: The list of target websites for the app can be seen in the CyberChef recipe here.
label: SOFTWARE

text: During our investigation into the Turla CyberAzov apps, we identified another Android app first seen in the wild in March 2022 that also claimed to conduct DoS attacks against Russian websites.
label: TIME

text: In this case, the Android app name was stopwar.apk (com.ddos.stopwar) and was distributed from the website stopwar.pro.
label: SOFTWARE

text: This app is quite different from the Turla apps described above and written by a different developer.
label: threat-actor

text: It also downloads a list of targets from an external site, but unlike the Turla apps, it continually sends requests to the target websites until it is stopped by the user.
label: threat-actor

text: Based on our analysis, we believe that the StopWar app was developed by pro-Ukrainian developers and was the inspiration for what Turla actors based their fake CyberAzov DoS app off of.
label: malware

label: vulnerability

text: As part of TAG's mission to counter serious threats to Google and our users, we've published analysis on a range of persistent threats including government-backed attackers, commercial surveillance vendors, and serious criminal operators.
label: identity

text: Today, we're sharing intelligence on a segment of attackers we call hack-for-hire, whose niche focuses on compromising accounts and exfiltrating data as a service.
label: attack-pattern

text: We have seen hack-for-hire groups target human rights and political activists, journalists, and other high-risk users around the world, putting their privacy, safety and security at risk.
label: attack-pattern

text: To help users and defenders, we will provide examples of the hack-for-hire ecosystem from India, Russia, and the United Arab Emirates and context around their capabilities and persistence mechanisms.
label: attack-pattern

text: Some hack-for-hire attackers openly advertise their products and services to anyone willing to pay, while others operate more discreetly selling to a limited audience.
label: attack-pattern

text: For example, TAG has observed Indian hack-for-hire firms work with third party private investigative services — intermediaries that reach out for services when a client requires them — and provide data exfiltrated from a successful operation.
label: location

text: This is detailed in depth in today’s Reuters investigation into the Indian hack-for-hire ecosystem.
label: location

text: We have also observed Indian hack-for-hire firms work with freelance actors not directly employed by the firms themselves.
label: location

text: The breadth of targets in hack-for-hire campaigns stands in contrast to many government-backed operations, which often have a clearer delineation of mission and targets.
label: attack-pattern

text: A recent campaign from an Indian hack-for-hire operator was observed targeting an IT company in Cyprus, an education institution in Nigeria, a fintech company in the Balkans and a shopping company in Israel.
label: location

text: Since 2012, TAG has been tracking an interwoven set of Indian hack-for-hire actors, with many having previously worked for Indian offensive security providers Appin and Belltrox.
label: TIME

text: One cluster of this activity frequently targets government, healthcare, and telecom sectors in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain with credential phishing campaigns.
label: location

text: These credential phishing campaigns have ranged from targeting specific government organizations to AWS accounts to Gmail accounts.
label: campaign

text: TAG has linked former employees of both Appin and Belltrox to Rebsec, a new firm that openly advertises corporate espionage as an offering on its company website.
label: identity

text: While investigating a 2017 credential phishing campaign that targeted a prominent Russian anti-corruption journalist, we discovered the Russian attacker targeting other journalists, politicians across Europe, and various NGOs and non-profit organizations.
label: TIME

text: This hack-for-hire actor has been publicly referred to as 'Void Balaur'.
label: attack-pattern

text: These campaigns were similar regardless of target, consisting of a credential phishing email with a link to an attacker-controlled phishing page.
label: attack-pattern

text: The lures ranged from fake Gmail and other webmail provider notifications to messages spoofing Russian government organizations.
label: location

text: After the target account was compromised, the attacker generally maintained persistence by granting an OAuth token to a legitimate email application like Thunderbird or generating an App Password to access the account via IMAP.
label: SOFTWARE

text: During our early investigation, TAG discovered the attacker’s public website (no longer available) advertising account hacking capabilities for email and social media services.
label: identity

text: The site claimed to have received positive reviews on Russian underground forums such as Dublikat and Probiv.cc.
label: DOMAIN

text: Over the past five years, TAG has observed the group targeting accounts at major webmail providers like Gmail, Hotmail, and Yahoo! and regional webmail providers like abv.bg, mail.ru, inbox.lv, and UKR.net.
label: identity

text: United Arab Emirates TAG is also tracking a hack-for-hire group now based in the United Arab Emirates that is mostly active in the Middle East and North Africa.
label: location

text: They have primarily targeted government, education, and political organizations including Middle East focused NGOs in Europe and the Palestinian political party Fatah.
label: location

text: The group commonly uses Google or OWA password reset lures to steal credentials from targets, often using the MailJet or SendGrid API to send phishing emails.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Unlike many hack-for-hire actors that use open source phishing frameworks like Evilginx or GoPhish, this group uses a custom phishing kit that utilizes Selenium, a self described 'suite of tools for automating web browsers.'
label: tools

text: Previously described by Amnesty, this phishing kit has remained under active development over the past five years.
label: identity

text: After compromising an account, the actor maintains persistence by granting themselves an OAuth token to a legitimate email app like Thunderbird, or by linking the victim Gmail account to an attacker-owned account on a third-party mail provider.
label: SOFTWARE

text: This group also has links to the original developers of H-Worm, also known as njRAT.
label: malware

text: In 2014, Microsoft filed a civil suit against the developer, Mohammed Benabdellah, for the development and dissemination of H-Worm.
label: TIME

text: Benabdellah, who also goes by the moniker Houdini, has been actively involved in the day-to-day development and operational deployment of the credential phishing capabilities used by this group since its inception.
label: attack-pattern

text: Upon discovery, all identified websites and domains were added to Safe Browsing to protect users from further harm.
label: SOFTWARE

text: We encourage any high risk user to enable Advanced Protection and Google Account Level Enhanced Safe Browsing and ensure that all devices are updated.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Additionally, our CyberCrime Investigation Group is sharing relevant details and indicators with law enforcement.
label: identity

text: TAG is committed to sharing our findings as a way of raising awareness with the security community, and with companies and individuals that might have been targeted.
label: identity

text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group tracks actors involved in disinformation campaigns, government backed hacking, and financially motivated abuse.

text: Since late 2019, our team has disrupted financially motivated phishing campaigns targeting YouTubers with Cookie Theft malware.
label: TIME

text: In collaboration with YouTube, Gmail, Trust & Safety, CyberCrime Investigation Group and Safe Browsing teams, our protections have decreased the volume of related phishing emails on Gmail by 99.6% since May 2021.
label: identity

text: With increased detection efforts, we’ve observed attackers shifting away from Gmail to other email providers (mostly email.cz, seznam.cz, post.cz and aol.com).
label: identity

text: Moreover, to protect our users, we have referred the below activity to the FBI for further investigation.
label: identity

text: Cookie Theft, also known as “pass-the-cookie attack,” is a session hijacking technique that enables access to user accounts with session cookies stored in the browser.
label: attack-pattern

text: While the technique has been around for decades, its resurgence as a top security risk could be due to a wider adoption of multi-factor authentication (MFA) making it difficult to conduct abuse, and shifting attacker focus to social engineering tactics.
label: attack-pattern

text: The phishing typically started with a customized email introducing the company and its products.
label: attack-pattern

text: Once the target agreed to the deal, a malware landing page disguised as a software download URL was sent via email or a PDF on Google Drive, and in a few cases, Google documents containing the phishing links.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Some of the websites impersonated legitimate software sites, such as Luminar, Cisco VPN, games on Steam, and some were generated using online templates.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Because Google actively detects and disrupts phishing links sent via Gmail, the actors were observed driving targets to messaging apps like WhatsApp, Telegram or Discord.
label: attack-pattern

text: We have observed that actors use various types of malware based on personal preference, most of which are easily available on Github.
label: SOFTWARE

text: Some commodity malware used included RedLine, Vidar, Predator The Thief, Nexus stealer, Azorult, Raccoon, Grand Stealer, Vikro Stealer, Masad (Google’s naming), and Kantal (Google’s naming) which shares code similarity with Vidar.
label: malware

text: Open source malware like Sorano and AdamantiumThief were also observed.
label: malware

text: We have a long-standing policy to send you a warning if we detect that your account is a target of government-backed phishing or malware attempts.
label: attack-pattern

text: So far in 2021, we’ve sent over 50,000 warnings, a nearly 33% increase from this time in 2020.
label: TIME

text: This spike is largely due to blocking an unusually large campaign from a Russian actor known as APT28 or Fancy Bear.
label: threat-actor

text: On any given day, TAG is tracking more than 270 targeted or government-backed attacker groups from more than 50 countries.
label: identity

text: In this blog, we explore some of the most notable campaigns we’ve disrupted this year from a different government-backed attacker: APT35, an Iranian group, which regularly conducts phishing campaigns targeting high risk users.
label: threat-actor

text: This is the one of the groups we disrupted during the 2020 US election cycle for its targeting of campaign staffers.
label: TIME
